h2: Ultrasonic testing myths that lead to missed flaws
html:
Ultrasonic testing myths that lead to missed flaws

These are the UT habits that look harmless on site and then fail an audit, or leave a flaw in service. Each comes down to calibration discipline, coverage or the scope of a technician's certification. The list across all five conventional methods is in conventional NDT myths.

Myth: Couplant is just there to wet the surface

Couplant is part of the calibration. Sound transfer into the part depends on the couplant's viscosity and the thickness of the layer under the probe, so a sensitivity set on the block with one couplant does not hold on the part with another. UT procedures written to ASME Section V typically require the same couplant for calibration and examination. On austenitic stainless steel, nickel alloys and titanium, chemistry matters too: procedures commonly cap sulfur and halides (chlorides plus fluorides) in the couplant at 250 ppm each, documented by the maker's batch certificate. On hot surfaces, use a couplant rated for the temperature, or the layer boils off mid-reading.

Myth: If the closing calibration check is off, the day's readings still count

The closing check exists to decide which data you keep. In procedures written to ASME Section V, when sensitivity has dropped beyond the procedure's tolerance, every data sheet since the last valid check is marked void and that area is examined again. When sensitivity has risen, the indications recorded since the last valid check are re-evaluated and re-recorded. That is why checks are made at the start, at the end of each examination or series, when personnel change and whenever part of the system changes. A technician who skips the closing check cannot show that any of the day's data was valid.

Myth: A gauge set up at room temperature reads hot pipe correctly

Sound travels more slowly in hot steel. A gauge whose velocity was set on a room-temperature block therefore reads a hot wall as thicker than it is, which is the unsafe direction for corrosion monitoring because the corrosion rate looks lower than it really is. Hot readings need a temperature correction or a calibration block at similar temperature, a high-temperature or delay-line probe, couplant rated for the surface, and short contact times so the probe does not heat up and drift. Record the surface temperature with every reading so the next survey of the same CMLs compares like with like. Ultrasonic pipe thickness testing explains how surveys are planned.

Myth: The straight-beam scan before angle-beam work is a formality

Weld UT procedures commonly require a straight-beam scan of the base metal the angle beam will pass through, and for good reason. A lamination in that path reflects or blocks the angle beam, so the weld volume behind it goes unexamined, or the lamination's echo is mistaken for a weld flaw. The scan is not an acceptance test of the plate. It maps where angle-beam results can be trusted and where another scan direction, another angle or another technique is needed. Mark laminated areas on the report so nobody assumes full coverage.

Myth: One scan direction from one side covers the weld

Angle-beam coverage depends on the beam angle, skip distance and access. Procedures written to ASME Section V Article 4 scan for reflectors parallel to the weld axis and for reflectors transverse to it. Parallel reflectors need scans across the weld from both sides where access allows; transverse cracks need scans along the weld, or across it on a ground-flush cap. Where only one side is reachable, as at a nozzle, a T-joint or a weld beside a flange, part of the volume is not covered and the report must say so. The scan plan belongs in the technique sheet a Level III approves; ultrasonic weld inspection shows how weld jobs are scoped.

Myth: A UT thickness certification covers weld examination

Thickness gauging and angle-beam flaw detection are different techniques with different skills. Many written practices certify thickness-only technicians under a limited certification with reduced training and experience, and that card does not cover shear-wave weld work. ASNT has said a written practice should address each technique the employer uses. Check the certification record for the technique, not just the letters "UT". For technicians moving up, ultrasonic testing training and NDT Level 2 training cover angle-beam theory, and the UT simulator lets them rehearse calibration and scanning before the hands-on practical at their own facility. For technique sheets and procedures, see NDT procedure development.
